lines: Picture a loop of currency conversions — dollars to euros, euros to pounds, pounds back to dollars.
Followed all the way around, it leaves more money at the end than the trip started with.
A real possibility for a few seconds on a real exchange. And exactly what a negative cycle means.
Bellman-Ford runs one more full round of relaxation, beyond what the vertex count already guarantees is enough.
Nothing anywhere improves.
Does that prove the graph has no negative cycle at all?
answer: Yes. A negative cycle would always find one more improving edge.

Every simple path has already stabilized by the time the guaranteed rounds are spent. One more round still improving something can only mean a cycle — and only a negative one keeps paying off forever.

lines: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge in the graph, on every round — not just the edges leaving one vertex.
It repeats that full pass a number of times tied to how many vertices the graph has, minus one.
No priority queue. No closest-first order. Just every edge, every round, until the count runs out.
Here's a chain built so each edge only helps the round after its neighbor already improved.
The correct distances only finish settling on the very last permitted round.
Proof the bound is tight, not just a safe overestimate.
Take that currency loop again, but weight each edge by the negative logarithm of its exchange rate.
A multiplying profit becomes an adding-up weight — one a shortest-path algorithm can actually read.
Run the algorithm, and the loop shows up as a negative cycle. Detected, and traced back edge by edge.
Here's a queue-driven variant. It only re-relaxes a vertex's outgoing edges when that vertex's own distance has just improved.
In the worst case, over every possible graph, does this ever cost strictly less than plain Bellman-Ford's fixed sweeps — or exactly the same amount?
answer: No. Its worst case is the identical bound as plain Bellman-Ford's.

On most graphs this skips a lot of wasted work. But build a graph where every correction arrives just late enough, and that rework compounds — until this variant relaxes more edges in total than the plain version ever would.

lines: Bellman-Ford answers the single-source question for any graph with a well-defined answer at all, negative edges included.
The one restriction Dijkstra needed is gone, at the cost of relaxing every edge instead of only the closest vertex's.
Running either algorithm once per vertex would answer a bigger question — but a cheaper way to pay that cost once, for the whole graph at once, is coming up next.
